promptText: Why does GraphQL solve REST's over-fetching and under-fetching problems, and what does it give up in exchange?
options: It replaces a fixed per-endpoint response shape with a client-declared query shape from one endpoint, but loses REST's free HTTP-level caching (ETags, Cache-Control)
It eliminates the need for a network round trip entirely by resolving everything on the client
It guarantees smaller payloads than REST because GraphQL responses are always compressed
It removes the need for a backend schema since the client defines its own types at request time
explanation: GraphQL fixes over/under-fetching by letting the client declare exactly the shape it needs from a single endpoint, but because it's typically served over POST, it forfeits native HTTP GET caching, which is why Apollo builds its own normalized client-side cache instead.

promptText: In a GraphQL schema, why is marking a field non-null (String!) risky when its resolver can legitimately fail?
options: A failure in a non-null field propagates the null up to the nearest nullable ancestor, potentially wiping out the entire parent object and any sibling data
Non-null fields are always resolved synchronously, so async resolvers can never be used on them
Non-null fields cannot be included in fragments or selection sets
Non-null fields automatically bypass Apollo's normalized cache and always hit the network
explanation: GraphQL's error-propagation rule nulls out the nearest nullable ancestor when a non-null field's resolver throws, so one flaky non-null field can silently erase an entire response subtree, including unrelated sibling data at that level.

promptText: What is the key execution-model difference between useQuery and useMutation in Apollo Client?
options: useQuery is declarative and fires automatically on mount or variable change; useMutation is imperative and only runs when its returned function is explicitly called
useMutation automatically retries failed network calls while useQuery never retries
useQuery only works with subscriptions, and useMutation only works with plain queries
Both hooks fire automatically on mount, but useMutation silently ignores any variables passed to it
explanation: useQuery runs declaratively whenever the component mounts or its variables change, while useMutation deliberately requires an explicit call (typically from an event handler) since you don't want a write operation firing just because a component rendered.

promptText: What is the actual difference between Apollo's network-only and no-cache fetch policies?
options: network-only always hits the network and still writes the result into the cache; no-cache always hits the network but never writes the result into the cache
network-only never touches the network at all, while no-cache always does
no-cache disables the query from ever executing
network-only only applies to mutations, and no-cache only applies to queries
explanation: Both policies always fetch from the network, but only network-only writes that response into the cache afterward — no-cache deliberately keeps the result out of the shared store, which is the detail interviewers use to catch shallow answers.

promptText: Why can a GraphQL response return HTTP 200 and still represent a genuine failure?
options: Errors are per-field: a resolver can fail for one nested field while the rest of the query resolves successfully, producing partial data alongside a populated errors array
Apollo Client always overrides the real HTTP status code with 200 regardless of outcome
GraphQL requires every response to use status 200 even when the request itself is malformed
Network-layer errors are silently converted into GraphQL-layer errors before the response is sent
explanation: GraphQL errors are field-level, not request-level, so a query can partially succeed — the response is still 200 OK with a data object containing whatever resolved plus an errors array pointing at what failed, violating the REST intuition that 200 means full success.

promptText: Why should a frontend engineer who never writes GraphQL resolvers still understand the N+1 problem?
options: Because the client's query shape and nesting depth directly determine whether the server's resolvers fan out into N+1 database calls
Because Apollo Client automatically applies DataLoader-style batching on the client with no server involvement
Because N+1 only happens when a GraphQL server is implemented as a thin wrapper around REST endpoints
Because the client, not the server, is responsible for writing and deploying the DataLoader batch function
explanation: In REST the backend controls what an endpoint fetches, but in GraphQL the client's query shape dictates the resolver call pattern the server executes — a deeply nested client query is effectively choosing to trigger N+1 fan-out unless the server has batching in place.

promptText: In an Apollo app, data from one order's line item mysteriously appears when viewing a completely unrelated order. What is the most likely root cause?
options: A LineItem type's default id-based cache key collides across orders because the id is only unique within its parent, causing different orders' items to silently overwrite each other in the normalized cache
The fetch policy is set to cache-and-network instead of cache-first
The GraphQL server is returning duplicate __typename values for every type
refetchQueries was never configured on the order-update mutation
explanation: If a type's id is unique only within its parent (like a line item's index inside an order), Apollo's default __typename:id cache key collides across parents; the fix is a custom keyFields composing a truly unique key, such as ["orderId", "id"].

promptText: Why would you prefer cache.modify over writeFragment when incrementing a post's like count after a mutation?
options: cache.modify lets you express the update as a transformation of the existing value (e.g. existing + 1) without first reading and reconstructing the full entity's data
cache.modify is the only cache API capable of updating the ROOT_QUERY pseudo-entity
writeFragment cannot target normalized entities, only whole query results
cache.modify automatically triggers a network refetch, unlike writeFragment
explanation: cache.modify's field functions receive the current cached value and let you return a derived new value directly, avoiding the read-then-spread-then-write dance writeFragment would require just to bump one field.

promptText: A posts(category, first, after) field is both filtered and paginated. How should keyArgs be configured to avoid both cross-category data bleeding and a paginated list splitting into disconnected fragments?
options: Include category in keyArgs so each category gets its own cache slot, and omit first/after so successive pages merge into one growing list per category
Include first and after in keyArgs so every page gets a unique slot, and omit category entirely
Set keyArgs to false so every category and page shares a single cache slot
Include category, first, and after in keyArgs to maximize cache key granularity
explanation: keyArgs should include arguments that change WHICH list is being viewed (filters like category) and exclude arguments that change WHERE you are within that same list (pagination cursors), letting the merge function concatenate pages within one filter's slot.

promptText: Mechanically, how does Apollo roll back a failed optimistic mutation without needing to compute a diff?
options: The optimistic response is applied as a separate, temporary layer on top of the base cache; on failure, that layer is simply discarded, and reads revert to the untouched base cache underneath
Apollo deep-clones the entire cache before every mutation and restores the clone on failure
Apollo re-runs every active query in the app from scratch whenever any mutation fails
Rollback requires the developer to manually call cache.evict inside the mutation's onError handler
explanation: Because the optimistic value was never merged into the base cache, only overlaid on top of it, 'rollback' is just removing that overlay — architecturally similar to an uncommitted database transaction rather than an undo of individual writes.

promptText: What specific bug does fragment masking prevent that plain fragment colocation (without masking) cannot?
options: A component accidentally reading a field it never declared in its own fragment, simply because a sibling fragment on the same normalized entity happened to fetch it — creating an invisible, undeclared coupling
A component sending malformed GraphQL syntax that the server rejects at parse time
Two sibling fragments defining the same field name with conflicting arguments in the same query
A query exceeding the server's configured maximum nesting depth
explanation: Without masking, fields from any fragment merged onto the same entity are all readable, so a component can silently start depending on a field only some other component's fragment declared; masking makes each component's data an opaque type until it unmasks only its own fragment's fields.

promptText: In a test using MockedProvider, why does an 'unmatched mock' failure usually point to a request-shape bug rather than a rendering bug?
options: MockedProvider matches mocks by exact query document and variables, so a failure means the component's actual outgoing request no longer matches what the mock expected, not that its render logic is broken
MockedProvider only checks that a component rendered without throwing an exception, ignoring the network request entirely
MockedProvider automatically falls back to hitting the real network whenever a mock goes unmatched
Unmatched mocks always indicate a missing ApolloProvider wrapper somewhere in the test tree
explanation: MockedProvider mocks the transport boundary with strict query-plus-variables matching, so an unmatched-mock error is a signal that the component's request shape drifted from what the test expects, distinct from a rendering defect.

promptText: Fragment A (a non-null title field whose resolver throws) and unrelated Fragment B (author name) are both spread into the same non-null `post` selection. What happens to Fragment B's data when Fragment A's field fails?
options: Fragment B's data is lost too, because null propagation operates on the response tree based on schema nullability, not on fragment boundaries — the failure nulls out the entire post object
Fragment B's data resolves normally because each fragment's fields are isolated from other fragments' failures
The server returns a 500 HTTP status instead of a partial GraphQL response
Apollo automatically retries only Fragment A's failing field while serving Fragment B's data from cache
explanation: Fragments are a client-authoring convenience invisible to the server's null-propagation rule; if the parent object (post) is non-null and one spread fragment's non-null field throws, the entire post object nulls out, taking down an entirely unrelated fragment's otherwise-successful data at the same level.

promptText: A team defines `export const userPrefsVar = makeVar(defaultPrefs)` at module scope and reuses that same module in a Node SSR server handling many concurrent requests. What bug does this introduce, and why?
options: The reactive variable becomes shared mutable state across the entire server process, so one user's render can leak into or overwrite a concurrent user's data — the fix is constructing the client (and its reactive variables) fresh inside a per-request factory
makeVar only works in browser environments and throws immediately when called from Node
Reactive variables cannot be read from inside a type policy's read function during server-side rendering
SSR mode automatically disables all reactive variables, so the variable is silently ignored with no effect
explanation: A top-level makeVar is a classic module-level mutable singleton — harmless in a single-user SPA but a cross-request data leak on a long-lived Node server handling many users concurrently, the same hazard as any other shared server-side singleton; the fix is a per-request factory function.

promptText: Relay makes fragment masking mandatory via a build-time compiler, while Apollo's masking (via GraphQL Code Generator) is opt-in. What deeper architectural trade-off does this reflect?
options: Relay pushes correctness properties like data-boundary enforcement into compile-time guarantees that scale with team size regardless of individual discipline, while Apollo favors runtime flexibility and incremental adoption at the cost of relying on convention and code review
Relay's masking is purely a bundle-size optimization with no effect on correctness, while Apollo's masking improves runtime rendering performance
Apollo's masking is strictly more rigorous than Relay's because it is configured declaratively through typePolicies rather than a compiler
Relay only supports masking for subscription operations, while Apollo supports it for queries and mutations
explanation: This is the deepest philosophical divide between the libraries: Relay's compiler statically guarantees consistency across every contributor at scale by making masking mandatory from inception, while Apollo's opt-in, retrofitted masking trades that guarantee for flexibility and an easier incremental-adoption path onto existing codebases.
